title: Klocek v. Gateway, Inc.
summary: Gateway failed to prove agreement to arbitrate; the court treated the enclosed terms as proposals to a nonmerchant rather than terms accepted merely by keeping the computer.
notes:
Court: U.S. District Court, District of Kansas (2000).

The notes report that Howard v. Ferrellgas Partners (2014) later described Kansas as adopting rolling formation. That later textbook report is kept separate from Klocek’s 2000 ruling and is not presented as a 2026 citator check. Five days here and thirty days in Hill are factual differences, but the decisions also disagree about formation, offeror identity, and § 2-207.

sections.Parties: Klocek brought individual and class claims against Gateway concerning support, compatibility, and warranties. Gateway sought dismissal in favor of arbitration.
sections.Material Facts: Gateway put a four-page Standard Terms document in the computer box. A conspicuous box on its first page purported to make retention beyond five days acceptance of the terms, including International Chamber of Commerce arbitration in Chicago. The evidence did not establish important details of the purchase or prior communication of the terms.
sections.Procedural History: The District of Kansas denied Gateway’s motion. Gateway had an initial summary-judgment-like burden to demonstrate an enforceable arbitration agreement and failed to supply adequate evidence. The court considered Kansas and Missouri law without resolving which governed, because neither route supported Gateway’s showing.
sections.Issue: Does § 2-207 apply despite only one written form, and did a consumer’s retention of the computer constitute express agreement to the enclosed arbitration term?
sections.Holding: Section 2-207 could apply. On the record and assumptions used for the motion, the customer offered to buy and Gateway accepted. The additional terms did not become part of the nonmerchant buyer’s contract without express agreement, which retention beyond five days did not establish.
sections.Reasoning: The statutory text and comment address oral agreements followed by written confirmation, so two exchanged forms are not a prerequisite. The vendor is not automatically the offeror merely because it supplies the goods. Gateway did not show it communicated an unwillingness to proceed without assent or alerted the customer at sale to the return-period condition. Shipment with terms was insufficient on this record. The court says the outcome would also follow under a proposed-modification analysis. Its procedural assumptions and incomplete record limit the decision’s reach.
